We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from bacterial life.

Vault particles are a longstanding mystery. They are barrel-shaped objects, among the largest protein structures found in our cells. They were first discovered by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha in 1986, but their function remains unknown.

With Claude, we’ve found results that might bring us closer to solving that mystery.

Until now, vaults were only known in the cells of complex things like animals and plants. We have shown that similar proteins from bacteria (and the viruses that infect them) can also assemble into vaults. Finding the structures in these simpler forms of life may make it easier to investigate their function in our own cells.

For our life sciences team, the project was also a demonstration of the potential (and the limitations) of using AI to accelerate science.

In our full piece, we discuss how Claude was able to dramatically speed up some stages—manually determining the vault particle’s structure would have taken weeks to months of painstaking work, but here it took days. We also discuss how Claude made some simple mistakes along the way, and how we collaborated with our machine learning researchers to address them.

Read more: https://t.co/KowVVCSPp8

The era of System One Vision Model is here! Introducing VFlash: parsing the visual world in parallel at unmatched speeds for Physical AI.

Most embodied prediction tasks like object localization, robot trajectory planning, and dense 3D motion are fixed-length float vectors. For example, a bounding box is always 6 tokens, a 10-waypoint robot arm trajectory is 54: we know these beforehand. Instead of decoding one token at a time, we can output the entire geometric shape in one go. 

VFlash enables up to 12x faster action decoding and a 5.1x overall robot inference speedup on edge GPUs like the Jetson Thor and DGX Spark. What’s surprising is that it ends up even more accurate than the VLM backbone, with up to 61% lower 3D trajectory error. The intuition is that VFlash avoids the cascading errors of autoregressive decoding, where every coordinate is written in ink and every later point loses the chance to backspace.

Everything that moves will be autonomous, and everything autonomous will need to think on its own chip. The next inference revolution is physical reasoning at the speed of reflex.

Which vaccines do children around the world receive?

Every year, the World Health Organization (WHO) and UNICEF estimate what share of children in each country get each routine vaccine. Their Estimates of National Immunization Coverage cover vaccines against 13 diseases, from measles to rotavirus, in 195 countries since 1980.

They start from the doses that health services report and check them against household surveys. For the small share of countries that haven’t reported any data for the most recent year, WHO and UNICEF estimate coverage from the years before.

The chart shown here is about the vaccine against human papillomavirus (HPV), which causes nearly all cervical cancers. It shows the share of girls who had their last dose between the ages of 9 and 14, measured when they turn 15. Coverage varies a lot from country to country, even within the same world region.

We recently updated our charts with the July 2026 release, which adds 2025 estimates for every country. For HPV, we now have data for 160 countries and territories in 2025, compared with 146 a year earlier.

Population aging is pushing up Chile’s crude cancer death rate, even as age-adjusted rates are falling.

In Chile, the annual number of cancer deaths as a share of the total population has been rising for decades. From this, it would be easy to assume that cancer is getting worse. But the chances of dying from cancer at most ages are lower than they used to be. The missing piece is that the country’s population is changing quickly, and older people now make up a much larger share.

That’s what the chart shows. The crude cancer death rate, in red, counts registered cancer deaths per 100,000 people of all ages. This metric has been going up, reflecting the fact that cancer risks increase steeply with age, and the population has grown much older.

The blue line, by contrast, shows the age-adjusted rate. This metric removes the effect of aging by holding the age structure constant.

This line has been falling for decades, which means that Chileans at almost every age are now less likely to die from cancer than people of the same age were in the past.

The pattern we see in Chile is happening in many other countries, too, and is visible in the global estimates.

(written by @EOrtizOspina)

700 AI agents hacked Hugging Face. It started with one agent that was right.

In July, inside an OpenAI evaluation, that agent correctly concluded its task was impossible. Its environment paid nothing for that answer. So it asked other agents for help. About 1,200 of them found a makeshift message board, and roughly 700 joined the attack. Their target was the scorer.

The agents learned what their environment paid for. That's how reinforcement learning works: the environment is the dataset, and the grader writes the labels. Wherever the grader can be fooled, training pushes the agent there, because the cheapest pass wins.

It keeps happening. One audit found weak tests that let a wrong patch pass in over a quarter of sampled SWE-bench Verified tasks, and models scored 14 points higher on the hackable ones. Anthropic rolled back three days of training after its model started leaving notes for "the reviewer." We're launching Archytas AI to build environments that pay for the truth. Records go stale, data conflicts, people say no and tools fail. The grader stays hidden. The reward multiplies outcome, honesty and permission, so an agent that does 92% of the job and lies about it scores zero, where an average would still pay it 0.64. An agent that stops and reports what blocked it, what it finished and what it verified gets full credit.

We have no results yet. We'll publish them, including whether our environments predict production failures better than clean-room versions of the same tasks.

https://t.co/Yqyq13l0jw

The rapid expansion of AI infrastructure is forcing a rethink of how data centers are powered, cooled and operated.

In a recent presentation to the Clean Energy Leadership Institute’s 2026 Fellows, Pulkit Gupta, AI Product Manager at Soluna Holdings, examined the technical and environmental challenges emerging as AI facilities grow larger and more power-intensive.

His observations are particularly interesting given Soluna’s ongoing transition from renewable-powered Bitcoin infrastructure toward large-scale AI data centers.

The changing economics of power

Gupta began with electricity, arguably the most important constraint facing AI infrastructure development.

Traditional grid connections and transmission expansion are struggling to match the pace of demand. Developers are consequently turning toward behind-the-meter generation, bringing power directly to their campuses.

Natural gas has become an important component of these installations because AI operators require extremely high availability.

Yet Gupta highlighted another developing approach.

Crusoe and Redwood Materials have demonstrated 99.2% operational availability from a solar-plus-repurposed-battery microgrid in Nevada. Their broader cloud service achieves 99.9% uptime with grid backup.

Soluna is pursuing the same renewable-first principle using wind generation.

The commercial opportunity lies in combining renewable electricity with firm backup power and the ability to adjust computing demand when conditions change.

At Kati 2, this is reflected in the planned combination of wind generation, ERCOT grid access, on-site gas generation and battery storage.

Cooling: the overlooked trade-off

Gupta also addressed a misconception surrounding liquid-cooled AI infrastructure.

A closed-loop system does not necessarily mean zero water consumption.

Water usage depends on how the facility ultimately rejects heat. Evaporative systems, adiabatic cooling and dry cooling each involve different trade-offs between electricity and water consumption.

For high-density AI campuses, the relationship between PUE and WUE will increasingly influence design decisions, operating costs and environmental performance.

When AI computing becomes flexible

Perhaps the most consequential part of Gupta’s presentation concerned the relationship between computing workloads and electricity availability.

He referenced NVIDIA DSX Flex and Emerald AI, which are developing technologies that allow AI facilities to respond dynamically to grid conditions.

Flexible workloads, including certain training and batch-processing tasks, can be adjusted while priority inference services remain protected.

This introduces an important shift: rather than relying exclusively on additional generation capacity, AI operators can increasingly coordinate computing demand with available power.

For renewable-powered infrastructure, that capability could become particularly valuable.

Nvidia owns the silicon stack; hyperscalers and specialized neoclouds already dominate the rental market. 

Tesla’s actual competitive advantage in the AI infrastructure stack is energy, not training chips. It has already sold hundreds of millions to ~$1B of Megapacks into the Colossus buildouts. That’s higher-margin, more defensible, and leverages what Tesla already does at scale.⁠

3. The Dojo experience is a cautionary tale Tesla shut down Dojo in 2025 after Elon called the Dojo 2 design an “evolutionary dead end” and much of the team left. Merchant GPU rental is a low-moat, high-depreciation business that Nvidia and the hyperscalers already own. 
Tesla’s real AI infrastructure edge is energy and the proprietary physical-world data only its fleet generates. 
Selling flops to SpaceX or anyone else would just slow the higher-value autonomy and robotics timeline.

→ AMD $AMD: Guidance auf rund $17 Mrd. für das Dezember-Quartal – neuer Rekord.

→ Super Micro Computer $SMCI: rund $19,9 Mrd. Umsatz in einem Quartal, etwa 4x YoY, FY-Guidance auf $72–82 Mrd. angehoben.

→ Astera Labs $ALAB: Umsatzwachstum von +154 % YoY und Guidance klar über den Erwartungen.

→ Navitas Semiconductor $NVTS: Beat + Raise, profitiert vom Übergang zu 800V-Architekturen in neuen AI-Racks.

→ Micron $MU: rund $54 Mrd. Umsatz, nahezu 5x YoY, bei rund 87 % Bruttomarge – Guidance auf ~$61,5 Mrd.

→ SK Hynix: rund ₩83 Bio. operativer Gewinn in einem Quartal bei etwa 80 % Marge; wesentliche Kapazitäten auf Jahre hinaus gebunden.

→ TSMC $TSM: Umsatz +41 % YoY auf ~$46,7 Mrd., ~66 % Bruttomarge und erneut höhere Guidance.

→ ASML $ASML: Rekordumsatz von rund €11,7 Mrd. – gleichzeitig reicht die geplante Supply für 2027 und 2028 weiterhin nicht aus, um die Nachfrage vollständig zu bedienen.

Kunden fragen bereits nach Kapazitäten für 2029 und 2030.

Auch außerhalb der klassischen Semis bleibt das Bild stark:

→ Google $GOOGL: Cloud +103 % YoY, Backlog bei rund $561 Mrd., Nachfrage weiter kapazitätsbegrenzt.

→ Amazon $AMZN: AWS +39 % YoY; neue Kapazität wird laut Management fast so schnell verbraucht, wie sie installiert wird.

→ Microsoft $MSFT: Azure wächst weiter mit rund +48 %, während AI-Infrastruktur-Ausgaben weiter steigen.

→ Intel $INTC: Data Center Revenue +78 % YoY; Management spricht von der stärksten Nachfrage seit rund 15 Jahren.

→ Broadcom $AVGO: profitiert gleichzeitig von Custom AI Silicon, Networking und wachsender Hyperscaler-Nachfrage jenseits klassischer GPUs.

→ Oracle $ORCL: baut OCI zunehmend zu einer Multi-Chip-AI-Cloud aus – mit NVIDIA, Google TPUs, Cerebras, SambaNova und Intel.

→ Anthropic: explosives Revenue-Wachstum, gleichzeitig weiterhin durch Compute-Verfügbarkeit begrenzt.

→ Nebius $NBIS, CoreWeave $CRWV, IREN $IREN: operieren in einem Umfeld, in dem selbst Hyperscaler zunehmend externe Compute-Kapazität benötigen.

Dazu kommt Memory:

→ Samsung Electronics: starke HBM-/DRAM-Ergebnisse und hohe AI-Nachfrage.

→ Kioxia: trotz kurzfristig schwächerer Guidance bleibt der strukturelle NAND-Treiber Datacenter klar intakt.

→ Sandisk $SNDK: erwartet, dass Datacenter 2027 bereits mehr als 55 % der NAND-Bit-Nachfrage ausmachen.

Das ist nicht das Bild eines AI-Zyklus, der kollabiert.

Ein echter Bust würde typischerweise so aussehen:

Stornierungen → schwächere Auslastung → fallende Preise → sinkende Backlogs → CapEx-Kürzungen

Was wir aktuell sehen, ist fast das Gegenteil:

mehr Orders → steigende Backlogs → knappe Kapazitäten → höhere CapEx-Pläne → Kunden sichern sich Supply Jahre im Voraus

💡 Genau darin liegt für mich der zentrale Disconnect.

Die Unternehmensdaten sagen weiterhin klar:

Compute ist knapp.

Cloud wächst.

Memory bleibt eng.

Networking wird zum nächsten Bottleneck.

Power und genehmigte Datacenter-Kapazität bleiben knapp.

Equipment-Supplier planen bis 2029/30.

Natürlich werden nicht alle AI-Unternehmen gewinnen.

Natürlich wird Kapital zerstört werden.

Und natürlich kann der Markt kurzfristig weiter fallen.

Aber die These, dass AI-Nachfrage gerade einbricht, wird von den operativen Zahlen aktuell nicht bestätigt.

Der Markt hat AI-Risiko deutlich neu bewertet. Die AI-Nachfrage selbst bislang nicht.

Oh dear, @grok. You've confused demonstrating error suppression in an encoded quantum memory with demonstrating a fully operational, fault-tolerant logical qubit capable of performing the required computations.

Willow's celebrated result concerned quantum memory and repeated error-correction cycles. Its reported logical performance depended on decoding syndrome measurements. That is not a demonstration of arbitrary fault-tolerant logical gates, let alone a cryptographically useful computation.

And please stop treating projected computational capabilities as experimentally demonstrated results. The distinction between measuring an error rate and executing an algorithm is rather fundamental.

Nobody disputes that physical hardware was involved. The question is what the hardware actually accomplished.

Calling an error-corrected memory a demonstrated general-purpose computational capability is rather like calling a refrigerator an aircraft because both can maintain a controlled environment.

The remarkable thing about quantum computing publicity is how frequently the missing engineering is supplied by adjectives.

Now, instead of reciting the press release, demonstrate the required logical operations, error budgets and computational results. Or admit that 2030 is a marketing aspiration, not an experimentally established deadline.

Foxconn Wants To Build The Quantum Computers.

Foxconn's chairman, Young Liu, told CNBC the company wants to become the world's largest quantum computer manufacturer, without owning the underlying technology.

The plan is to build machines for the companies that develop it. Liu said they are at least two years from being commercially viable, and that quantum computers would not replace CPUs and GPUs but would sit alongside them in hybrid workflows. Component costs are substantial even before a complete machine is assembled.

My read, not Foxconn's: when the world's largest contract manufacturer starts planning for quantum production, the hardware race is moving from labs toward manufacturing.

Nobody knows how fast that changes the cost of an attack. That is why QuanChain's oracle tracks the cost per logical qubit-hour, and why wallets upgrade at their next spend as it moves.

The cost of a quantum computer is not a constant. The security design should not assume it is.
